articles.text: They journeyed from Rephidim, entered the wilderness of Sinai, and camped in the wilderness; Israel camped there in front of the mountain. Exodus 19:2 We live in a world of frequent goodbyes. To be human is to say goodbye to places we have come to appreciate, to say goodbye to ways of being we have grown accustomed to, to say goodbye to people we have come to love. As the people of old journey towards Sinai, they must say goodbye to Rephidim. In the biblical narrative Rephidim was a place of both human need and God’s provision. It was a place where humans questioned both God and Moses. They wondered if God knew what God was doing and they wondered if they could trust the leadership of Moses. At Rephidim God provided water to the easily distracted, easily disgruntled congregation. Rephidim was a place of both pain and provision. Inevitably, the people were called to move beyond both the memory of the pain and the security of the provision. They were to move on to new experiences, new challenges and new revelation. They were to move on carrying the lessons they are learned and the experiences they are shared. They were to say goodbye to Rephidim but never to forget it. As the people say goodbye, God, through Moses, tells them that they are being carried on eagles’ wings. As they say goodbye they are promised not protection but presence. One of the most visited exhibits at the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago was the painting “Breaking Home Ties” by Thomas Hovenden. The poignant scene shows a young man beginning his life’s journey as he bids farewell to his family. Many wept openly before the painting because it portrayed the goodbyes they had come to know so well. We too are a people that have said many goodbyes. There are goodbyes behind us, before us and between us. Let us not take them lightly but let us not let them crush us for, as hard as they are, as real as they are, the eagles’ wings that carry us are also real, the Divine Presence that surrounds us is also real, leading us through, rather than around, our many goodbyes to places of insight, understanding, courage and hope. God bless this broken road of many goodbyes. May our goodbyes be our promise to never forget, to trust in the wings that bear us up. In the closing words of Blest Be the Ties That Bind, “When we asunder part it gives us inward pain. But we shall still be joined in heart and hope to meet again.” Pastor Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church at Lakeshore Avenue and Mandana Boulevard in Oakland.

She is the warm smile that greets you when you walk through the doors of the PRD building, the cheerful voice on the other end of the phone, and the ‘glue’ who has helped make all things PRD feel a little more magical,” said Supervisor Eva Phalen of the Recreation Department and a member of the July 4 parade committee. “I’ve worked with this committee closely for so many years. I respect what they do; they’ve given up so much time and I know that they don’t freely choose just anybody to be Grand Marshal,” said Wood. Wood grew up in Piedmont and first appeared in the parade with the Bluebirds and Campfire Girls when she was a Beach school student. The Rec Department’s rich involvement with the parade has meant that Wood has been to or been a part of around 30 Piedmont parades. Wood helped run the Fourth of July Pancake Breakfast for six years, when the Recreation Department inherited the event from the Montclair-Piedmont Rotary Club. Wood will be on the judging stand this year to vote for the parade winners and she gave some clues to float builders on how to win her favor. “I love the creative ones, and the neighborhood ones. I will vote for the floats that think outside the box,” she said. “Independence Day the Piedmont Way” is the parade theme this year, the 59th annual parade. Wood’s involvement in so many past parades will ensure that this one has that special Piedmont touch. articles.text: Work began on Monday, June 15, as the final phase of the city’s Civic Center parking reconfiguration project. The project constitutes the reconfiguration of Bonita Avenue between Vista and Oakland Avenues. This project will: • Convert the Havens Elementary side of the street from parallel parking to diagonal parking and remove the dropoff zone. • Add two new ADA parking spaces. • Convert this block of Bonita to one-way traffic, going toward Oakland Avenue. When completed, the work will create 17 new parking spaces, split between Permit A (PUSD employee) and time-limited (2-hour). The work is expected to take three to four weeks. Demolition for the new ADA ramp began on Monday. Next week, the city plans to begin grading the ADA spaces and pouring new ramps, and then the final step will be striping and signage. Previous phases of this project included a new drop-off zone on Highland Avenue across the street from Havens Elementary in January, and new time-limited parking spaces on Bonita and Magnolia in April. The city’s stated goals for the Civic Center parking reconfiguration project are to provide a better parking experience for visitors, while also reducing congestion and improving pedestrian safety. The plan was approved by the city council last summer after a series of discussions spanning several council meetings. Construction work starts on Bonita Ave. Construction workers demolish the curb to build a new ADA ramp for Havens School.
articles.title: City begins work on Civic Center parking reconfiguration project

articles.text: Handsome Jonas and Austin are looking for a calm home where they can continue growing into the affectionate companions they’re meant to be. Both one-year-olds start off shy, which makes it extra-rewarding to patiently watch their trust blossom day by day. Jonas is the more playful of the pair. He loves wand toys, treats, and lap time. Although initially quite timid, he transforms into a loving companion who enjoys being part of the action and spending time with people. Austin may hide briefly when he’s feeling nervous, but once he settles in, he’s affectionate, playful, and a truly wonderful friend. He enjoys lounging by the window and pouncing on his favorite toys. Austin also has FIV, so he will need to stay inside, but fear not: cats with FIV can live long, happy lives with routine veterinary care, and can live safely alongside cats without FIV. Give them a bit of extra time to settle in and they’ll form a deep bond you’ll cherish. Jonas and Austin are neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV negative. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council agreed on June 15 to place a measure increasing the property transfer tax rate on Piedmont’s November ballot. The proposed ordinance would increase the transfer tax from 1.3% to 1.75%, better aligning Piedmont’s rate with neighboring cities and generating an additional $1.5 million annually. The ballot measure would require a majority vote to pass. The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee examined funding mechanisms to address the city’s deferred maintenance obligations, capital infrastructure needs, and longterm revenue sustainability. The advisory recommended that the council consider increasing the property transfer tax. If approved by voters in November, this would be the first time Piedmont’s property transfer tax has been changed in 33 years. According to the Financial Planning Committee, around 10% of the total budget is funded by the property transfer tax. The city uses the funds for capital investment and maintenance of aging facilities, buildings, and infrastructure systems. This vote was the first step in the process of placing a measure on the November ballot. A second vote is tentatively scheduled for the council’s July 6 meeting, at which time the council would have the ability to make changes to the proposed new tax rate. The deadline to submit materials to the Alameda County Registrar of Voters for the November ballot is August 7.

articles.text: The “Local Taxpayer Act” is anticipated to be on the ballot for the California statewide election this November. This act would strip charter cities of their authority to impose certain taxes on real estate. Additionally, it would require that all local special taxes obtain two-thirds voter approval, and it would invalidate certain existing taxes that were previously approved by voters. Charter cities can adopt laws concerning “municipal affairs” that differ from state statutes. As a charter city, Piedmont can impose a property transfer tax to generate funds for the city. If this authority is taken away, it would significantly affect Piedmont’s ability to finance facility maintenance and capital improvements. “For the last 15 years, we’ve used the transfer tax to fund important things the city needs to do, like replace equipment, maintain facilities, and provide for capital improvements. Without the transfer tax, the funds we’ve established for those categories would begin to be exhausted,” said budget advisory committee member Robert McBain, a former mayor and city council member. Around 10% of Piedmont’s budget is funded by the property transfer tax, or $4.2 million. Without these funds, the city would have to significantly decrease its investment into facility management, equipment replacement, and capital projects. “There’s not a lot of flexibility in the budget, and if you’re going to take out $4 million, it would significantly impact core operations,” McBain continued. “I think in a couple of years, we will begin to see a deterioration in the city’s physical infrastructure, equipment, and things like that, which will only impede core operations. To say it would be disruptive would be an understatement. It would be disruptive in the short term, and the city’s financial condition would be damaged,” said McBain. To make up for the revenue lost from the removal of the property transfer tax, Piedmont would need to go to voters for tax or fee increases. McBain believes even if the city did this, it would not replace the lost revenue from the transfer tax. The city is part of the California League of Cities, an organization that advocates for the local rights of all cities in California. Currently it is lobbying to remove the act from the November ballot. They sent a letter to the key lawmakers warning that a ballot measure sponsored by the California Business Roundtable and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association could result in local service cuts for Californians. State law allows proponents to withdraw an initiative 131 days before the November general election. Cal Cities is working to remove the initiative before the June 25 deadline.
articles.title: How a November ballot act could negatively impact Piedmont

articles.text: Mira Sachs delivered a speech during the PHS Class of 2026’s Commencement Ceremony as the Student Speaker. Sachs was selected by the school board as a student representative to the board last year, and will attend Vanderbilt University in the fall. It feels strange to be celebrating this huge milestone here in this very spot because, since elementary school, I would celebrate the days I wouldn’t have to be on this track. I hated running the mile, and I wasn’t alone. Most of us would finish each lap begrudgingly, complaining on our way back to class about how we would have to do it again next week. But there were always the kids like Arden Sorensen-Wald and Henry DeVan who not only loved it but wanted to win. Ask them their mile time — I’m sure they still remember it. So you can imagine how I felt at freshman year orientation, sitting right here, when the speakers opened their presentation with the metaphor of running the mile: four laps and four years. And now I get it; the first lap seemed easy, lap two we had to pick up the pace, lap three barely happened but hurt the most, and on lap four all most of us thought about was the end. But now that I’m here, what I’ve discovered is that the best approach isn’t just aiming for the finish line. Even though we are at the end, I know that life will continuously offer us races: to graduate college, to get a dream job, to find a partner, to have a family. Running towards the next finish line is what keeps us sane. But the tendency to divide life into equal segments causes its meaningful moments to get lost. It’s how things inevitably go by too quickly. My mom likes to say that turning 50 is like becoming the freshman of old age — which I disagree with — but we will be freshmen, sophomores, juniors and seniors in some variation for the rest of our lives. Obviously many of us will be freshmen again next year and all the parents in the audience right now are seniors of raising children so congrats to you too, but you’re about to go through freshman orientation of supporting young adults, so don’t go thinking your race is over just yet. And Class of 2026 - neither is ours. There is a circular nature to life and it will continue to unfold as quickly as we let it. Although all of these milestones will be exciting, I do not want to just look forward to the next one. Instead, I have decided that I am going to find the right pace – and I am encouraging you all to find yours. Here are some memories from running the mile that made it more enjoyable, and if applied to life, might make it feel less like a race and more like living. slowed things down for them but it created a stronger moment to remember. So many people in Piedmont have modeled kindness for us. Mr. Hartford regularly makes days feel special with his birthday raps. Dr. Yoshihara greets us with a fist bump and addresses all 179 of us by name. And Ms. Black does exercise breaks in class when she recognizes it’s too early on a Thursday morning for Old English. I couldn’t possibly list all the kindness our mentors here have shown, but those moments stand far apart from all the random days that disappeared in our race to get here today. The next lesson I learned from the mile is that if you’re going to fake an injury, make sure it’s only you and maybe one other friend, not the whole friend group- that’s a dead giveaway. But… I’m not quite sure how that applies to life so let’s move on. My final lesson learned from the mile is to wear what makes you happy. Some people would show up in running shoes and others dared to try something new, running in colorful converse, sparkly sneakers, or if they were really bold, crocs. During our final lap I watched my classmates do exactly that. From impressive outfits, to people decked out in gear for rallies or bright smiles, this class dares to be themselves. Days can blur together if we don’t carefully consider how we show up. Whether that’s attire, attitude, or approach — what matters is being intentional. We’ve had a great run, Class of ‘26, and I’m so grateful to have done these four laps with you. How we showed up on this track said something about who we were becoming, and now, at a new place, in a new chapter, we get to decide that all over again. Running naturally separates people, and not always into usual friend groups - often just by people’s paces. My mile friends weren’t always my usual friends but they were still my speed in a different sense. Running with people outside our usual pack can open our mind to new perspectives and experiences, and takes us away from the comfortable but narrow reality of always engaging with the same few people. Kindness makes experiences more meaningful: At the track, Mr. Wiz and Mr. Best always played just the right music to push us through which also built community. I remember that for one mile someone forgot her sneakers. And the girl’s friend generously offered her one of her sneakers in exchange for the others’ flip flop. Together, they hobbled around the track in mismatched shoes…this literally

articles.text: PHS Salutatorian Niko Kalamas will attend Dartmouth College in the fall. Seniors, here we are on the last day of school. We made it through what we thought might take us forever, and look at the view that we have. Here on the field in the late afternoon, we get to look back on our home upon the hill of the past four years. I think it is unique because it is not often a graduating class gets such a perfect view of where we came from. I am grateful for it. we learned about the chaparral biome we live in and how weather affects our area. In Econ we had the Urban Plan project, bringing tangible opportunities to see how cities like San Francisco get mapped and built. Like PE hill, these challenges gradually got steeper, but we were not fazed and took advantage of the opportunities they presented. Preparation also came through our community. These hikes were only made easier together and allowed us to get to the top while realizing the value of connection. Classes at Piedmont felt more like conversations the older we got, from sharing answers to Mr. Palsa’s warm-up questions to full group discussions about Hamlet with Dr. Marks. Mr. C highlighted his wall of school pennants, showing all of the former students he connected with, and all the counselors always ran through the halls checking in with everyone. That tight-knit environment was what transformed our daunting mountains into rolling hills. This is our last day here. Which means we have more to look forward to. While I could not be more grateful for the climbs Piedmont had to offer, it is time to join our families and staff and look towards what lies next. Graduates, could you please stand up? Now, turn to face the city. Look at that view. Out there are more challenges, more new experiences, more hills. Please now be seated. Our time here has made us conditioned to conquer everything out there and I think I am not alone in feeling grateful for the obstacles ahead. We are all prepared for what lies beyond. Thank you. That hill that might be blocking our classrooms from view has been more than just a feature of the landscape. Over the past four years it has been our favorite obstacle that we learned to overcome. Whether that was on our walk to school, after running the mile during freshman PE, sports events down here at Witter or the baseball field, or going home after Day on the Green, we made this climb a routine in our lives. I am thankful we were tasked with this challenge from day one because it served as good practice for everything that followed. Whether we were aware of it or not, what did follow was preparation for our time beyond high school. In freshman English we were pushed to be curious about the world with the I-Search project. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District has reached tentative agreements extending contracts through 2029 for both the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) and California School Employees Association (CSEA). The new contracts will give teachers and staff 3-4% raises next year, a 3% raise in 2027 and another 3% raise for the 2028-29 year. Teachers voted in favor of the contracts on Friday, June 5 and the board plans to approve the updated agreements in its meeting tonight, June 17. “Nothing short of a miracle. The work required was monumental,” said APT President Elise Marks. “I want to say a profound thank you to the district management negotiating team that worked with APT.” For the 2026-2027 school year, all employees will receive a one-time bonus of $2000. The new contract also works to attract new teachers by bumping up the salary schedule for new teachers in each of their first five years. Previously, teacher salaries were stalled in their first five years. In the previous contract the minimum salary for full-time teachers was $71,576. Next year the minimum salary will increase to almost $74,000, and by 2028- 2029 it will be over $78,000. “These agreements reflect the things that this board and our labor partners have consistently stood for, which are competitive and sustainable compensation, affordable and high-quality healthcare, low class sizes, and the long-term fiscal health of the district,” said School Board President Ruchi Medhekar in the June 3 meeting. Kim Randlett led the negotiating team for the district along with Chief Business Officer Ruth Alahydoian and Stephanie Griffin. Marks thanked the district’s negotiation team for their hours at the table with APT negotiators “really listening, really wrestling with the issue, brainstorming possible solutions and compromises,” she said. “It’s my profound desire to pay teachers, who I believe are chronically underpaid throughout this country, as much as we responsibly can. And I think we’re working on that. I won’t say we’re all the way there, but we’ve made strides,” said board member Max Roman. Teachers were advocating for a return to the 2010 policy of fully-paid family healthcare coverage. The district couldn’t grant that request with rising healthcare costs, but the agreement will increase the district’s contribution to health benefits by 25% over the next two years. This agreement will grant four weeks of paid parental leave within the first year of a new child’s birth, adoption, or the start of foster care. “Most people don’t know that California teachers don’t have access to state disability and don’t get any paid parental leave, so have always had to use up their personal sick leave to stay home even briefly with a newborn,” explained Marks. The agreement does not give teachers their desired hard caps on maximum class sizes, but the parties agreed in principle to try to bring down some of the extreme class sizes. “District administration has clearly been making good faith efforts to do so, and we very much appreciate the changes so far. Students will feel the difference next year,” said Marks about class size. The agreement grants a wish from the parents clubs, and the contract now obliges teachers to make “every reasonable effort” to grade student work “within 15 school days of the due date (or from the date of submission for work accepted late).” This new agreement is projected to cost the district an additional $1,533,765 for teachers and $684,478 for CSEA employees next year. The cumulative increased cost in compensation for both groups for the next three years is projected at $4,581,671 - $1,404,298 for CSEA and $3,177,373 for teachers. articles.text: Piedmont High School seniors participated in the second annual Cap and Gown Day on May 27 by donning their purple graduation attire and heading back to their elementary schools. The students reunited with former teachers at Beach, Wildwood and Havens schools and enjoyed hanging out with elementary school students. The event was started in 2025 by Dean Olliphant and Juliana DeYoung and has quickly become a new tradition. This year the students leading the organization of the event were Luke McAuliffe, Lila Rosen, Grace Alonigreen, Sydney Olson, Zachary Dupree and Vivian Burke Class of 2026 graduates who entered the school district during middle or high school were allowed to pick a school to visit. At Havens, the cap and gown graduates walked around Becker Field as a parade, high fiving the elementary school students and hugging former teachers. At Wildwood the Class of 2026 took over the jungle gym and played games on the blacktop. At Beach, returning graduates sat in their former classrooms but this time took to the front of the room with their teachers. Cap and Gown Day, during the second to last week of school, served as a primer coalescing K-12 memories before saying goodbye to Piedmont schools. articles.text: STEM programs are available at Oakland Space Academy this summer Sunday, June 21, marks the official start of astronomical summer in the Northern Hemisphere. This means that the Sun is shining directly on the Northern Hemisphere, and we experience the warm, sunny weather of summer. At Chabot, summer fun is in full swing with plenty of activities and programs. The Oakland Space Academy, the workforce development sector of Chabot, has developed several exciting STEM programs this summer to build knowledge, skills and community. Oakland Space Academy The Oakland Space Academy (the Academy) is Chabot’s STEM workforce development program. The Academy provides high school students and recent high school graduates with the knowledge, skills, and experiences needed to obtain, retain, and advance in education and employment. It helps prepare students for successful transitions into postsecondary education and careers through training, career exploration, work-based learning, support services, and employer engagement. The Academy is offering several exciting courses this summer which will provide students with the opportunity to develop scientific thinking, technical skills, and career readiness through authentic scientific investigation. The Academy’s summer of learning This summer, the Oakland Space Academy is hosting several STEM-based courses for students. Starting on June 22nd, the Academy is beginning a weeklong course called Quantitative Solar Spectroscopy: The Fate of Our Sun. In this course, students will explore ways to learn about the Sun and other stars. Through hands-on investigation, they will learn the principles of spectroscopy, collect and analyze spectral data, and compare the composition and characteristics of our Sun to other stars. Students will also gain firsthand experience using Chabot’s historical telescopes during a nighttime observation session, applying the same techniques scientists use to study objects across our galaxy. Oakland Space Academy courses strengthen foundational STEM knowledge by applying concepts from astronomy, physics, chemistry, mathematics, and data science. Join Chabot’s Summer of Fun For those who are not in the Oakland Space Academy and are within grades 8 to incoming 12th graders, Oakland Space Academy courses are available for enrollment. Visit chabotspace.org for more information about the Academy and to see all Chabot has to offer this summer! Cameron Schneider is with Chabot Space and Science Center in Oakland. articles.text: We’re still getting through the 2026 FIFA World Cup’s opening matches of the Group Stage with some surprises thus far. Perhaps one of the largest revelations happened in Group D with the United States putting a 4-1 whooping on Paraguay and Australia upsetting Turkiye 2-0. Note: Opening matches for Groups J, K, and L were not complete by Post time. Here’s how things are going, starting with the U.S. Group D. Group D: United States (3 points), Australia (3 points), Turkiye (0 points), (0 points) Paraguay How spectacular was the US’ performance against Paraguay. Their quality cannot be undervalued; leading 3-nil at halftime, plus a fourth goal that featured 26 consecutive passes before Gio Reyna’s trivela finish. Paraguay, meanwhile, isn’t bad—they beat Mexico 2-1 back in November. The United States can actually clinch the group by beating Australia this Friday, June 19 and a loss or draw by Turkey against Paraguay. As for the Aussies, we had them finishing third in the Group but could exceed those expectations after its dominant win over Turkey. If they lose to the US, the Socceroos can still get second place in the Group with Paraguay dropping points to Turkey. Group A: Mexico (3 points), South Korea (3 points), Czechia (0 points), South Africa (0 points) Mexico had a strong 2-nil opening win over South Africa, which looked like one of the worst teams in the tournament. South Korea rallied for a 2-1 win over Czechia, keeping my predictions alive. Czechia will now face South Africa, which is looking like a must-win for the European side to make it out of the group. Group B: Switzerland (1 point), Canada (1 point), Qatar (1 point), Bosnia & Herzegovina (1 point) It’s even as it gets for Group B with each of Canada vs. Bosnia, and Qatar vs. Switzerland playing to 1-1 ties. The group returns to action on June 18 with the Swiss facing Bosnia and Canada playing Qatar. I have Switzerland winning the group, Canada taking second, and Bosnia claiming a third-place, and it could certainly go in any direction at this point. Group C: Scotland (3 points), Brazil (1 point), Morocco (1 point), Haiti (0 points) Scotland seized its opportunity over low ranked Haiti with a 1-nil win, while Brazil and Morocco played to a 1-1 draw in one of the most entertaining matches of a very fun Group Stage opening game. I still think Brazil will take control of the group and will handle Haiti on June 19, while Morocco will jump in front of Scotland the same day. Group E: Germany (3 points), Ivory Coast (3 points), Ecuador (0 points), Curaçao (0 points) Germany crushed Curacao 7-1 to take command of the group, but it looks like Ivory Coast will spoil my prediction for the group by beating Ecuador 1-0. Germany faces Ivory Coast on June 20, giving Ecuador a chance to climb back in contention against Curacao. If Ivory Coast can take points against Germany, that may punch their 2E ticket. Group F: Sweden (3 points), Netherlands (1 point), Japan (1 point), Tunisia (0 points) Sweden put an impressive 5-1 stamp on Tunisia to put itself in the conversation to win the group. The Netherlands and Japan, meanwhile, played to a highly entertaining 2-2 draw. I picked Holland to take 1F, Japan in 2F, and Sweden in a third-place spot. The match to watch is the Dutch playing the Swedes on June 20, as it will have a major impact on the group’s outcome. Group G: New Zealand (1 point), Iran (1 point), Belgium (1 point), Egypt (1 point) Group favorites Belgium played to a tightly contested 1-1 tie with Egypt. Iran and New Zealand battled to a 2-2 result and lead the group by goals scored. My prediction is still alive with Belgium facing Iran on June 21, but if they fail to win, it could be all she wrote. articles.text: The 2025-26 school year has officially concluded at Piedmont High with teams turning the page on another sports calendar. In this article, the Post reflects on our favorite moments from the recent sports seasons. Boys’ Swimming 200 medley team places ninth at CIF State Piedmont High’s boys’ swimming team put together a monster 2026 spring campaign. Nik Costello proved to be a vital part of the boys’ swimming team’s record-setting year as a senior leader of the bunch. He helped lead Piedmont High’s 200 medley relay team to the CIF State Championship on May 16, coming away with the school’s firstever medal in the prestigious meet’s 12-year history, placing ninth of 18 schools with a time of 1:33.56 alongside Asher Takazawa, Connor Carnazzo, and Jeffrey Latronica. He shutout St. Patrick’s Oscar Swenson 6-0, 6-0 in the opening round, won 6-1, 6-4 over Armaan Mishra of Lick-Wilmerding in the quarterfinals, and beat Stuart Hall’s Edward Morfit 6-1, 6-0 in the semifinals. articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School softball team’s season came to a close as the team faced off against two big rivals in back-toback games. On Tuesday, May 26, the Scots took the field one last time in the East Bay Middle School League Championship against rivals from across Hwy 13, the Montera Middle School Toros. After a rousing rendition of the National Anthem led by player representatives from each team, the game got underway. As was often the case throughout the season, pitching was once again the star of the show as 8th grade aces Madi Farboud and Bailey Gregovich would end up throwing a combined no-hitter through six nail-biting innings. The duo stifled the Toros normally potent offense allowing zero earned runs and posting nine strikeouts against a team that previously averaged 13 runs per game. The score was tied 2-2 through six innings thanks to aggressive base running from Bailey Gregovich and 6th grader Cate Penrod, who each took advantage of some sloppy throws to score on close plays at the plate. The Scots dugout was charged up as the game headed to the extra frame but alas their championship dreams would be undone by a passed ball and a fielder’s choice that allowed the winning run for Montera to score in the bottom of the seventh. Also on Monday, May 25, they played an annual exhibition game that once again pitted the players against the parents and coaches in a Memorial Day matchup at Witter field. With the all-time series knotted at 1-1, the Non-Kids looked to have a secure 8-3 lead heading into the final inning before giving up 5 runs in an error-filled 5th that ended the game in a tie. The adults still claimed a moral victory however as all were able to leave the field under their own power and injury-free. The 2026 softball season represented only the second year of the Middle School program. The Scots closed the season as the runner-up in both leagues that they played in this season, finishing 13-4, and they were the only team to win a match against the Toros (16-1). As the 8th grade leaders Abby Gregovich, Bailey Gregovich, Madi Farboud, Sarina Hill, and Simone Tornatore move on to Piedmont High School next year, the Scots look forward to continued strong contributions from players like rising 8th grader Mackenzie Ewen (.515 avg/16 RBI) and rising 7th graders, Keira Spina (.462 avg/12 RBI) and Clara Blanchard (10 RBI) next spring. Pitchers Madi Farboud (left) and Bailey Gregovich threw a combined no-hitter against Montera. Mackenzie Ewen hit .515 in her second season with the Scots. articles.text: Yaxel Lendeborg The 2026 NBA season has officially come to an end with the New York Knicks crowned as this year’s champions. Now that the finals are behind us, the sporting world is looking toward the NBA Draft. The first round takes place on June 23, with the second round on the following day. As the Warriors reach the end of the Steph Curry era, the margin of error is shrinking, and the need to get this draft right is paramount. They missed the playoffs this past season after losing to the Phoenix Suns in the play-in tournament. The team’s needs include wing depth, a center, and a shooting guard. Below are three names the Warriors should consider at the eleventh pick to address their needs. 1. Yaxel Lendeborg Forward, Michigan Lendeborg is best known for leading Michigan to the NCAA championship this past season. He’s 6’8 and plays a mix of small forward and power forward. He averaged 15 points, seven rebounds, and three assists per game, while shooting 51% from the field. Scouts say Lendeborg is an all-around player who can defend at a very high level, and space the floor with his threepoint shot. The only downside to Lendeborg is his age. At 23 years old, many believe there isn’t much more development for him, and he’s likely close to his ceiling. Lendeborg addresses a serious need for wing talent on the Warriors roster and can play right away on a team that’s hoping to get back into the playoff hunt. 2. Aday Mara Center, Michigan Mara is a 7’3 center who was an integral part of Michigan’s title-winning season. Mara averaged 12 points, seven rebounds, two assists, and two blocks per Photo courtesy of University of Michigan game. His best trait is his ability to protect the rim. He’s expected to immediately be one of the best rim-protecting big men in the NBA. Mara’s ability to pass has impressed many scouts, who don’t often see a seven-foot big guy able to pass like a point guard. Mara’s defensive dominance and offensive upside provide the Warriors with a legit center that they haven’t had since 2016 with Andrew Bogut. Photo courtesy of University of Arizona Brayden Burries 3. Brayden Burries Shooting Guard, Arizona Burries stands out as a scoring shooting guard with the potential to be a secondary point guard. He averaged 16 points, five rebounds, and 2 assists per game while shooting 39% from threepoint range. According to many scouts, Burries’ best attribute is his shooting ability. He has a quick first step when driving towards the rim and doesn’t shy away from contact. He would fit nicely into the Warriors’ starting lineup next to Steph Curry. As the Warriors look to address numerous needs through this offseason, fans can only hope general manager Mike Dunleavy Jr. gets it right. Aday Mara Photo courtesy of University of Michigan

articles.text: An exhibition featuring work by Oakland-based artist Demetri Broxton, entitled Demetri Broxton: Ancestral Echoes, is on view now at the Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco. Broxton is one of four artists selected as part of MoAD’s 10th cohort of annual Emerging Artists Program (EAP) for 2026- 2027. The 2026-2027 awardees were selected from hundreds of applicants and present single artist shows at MoAD from now through early 2027. “Each of the 2026-2027 recipients have a deep reverence for ancestral legacies, Black futurity, and the interplay of personal and collective histories,” Key Jo Lee, MoAD Chief of Curatorial Affairs and Public Programs, said in a press release. “Their exhibitions at MoAD will be significant contributions to their respective mediums, and represent crucial milestones for their long-term practices.” Ancestral Echoes is an ongoing body of work that traces the Demetri Broxton artist’s family’s movement across the American South to Oakland. Broxton, who is of Louisiana Creole and Filipino heritage, uses screen-printed textiles, beadwork, cowrie shells, sequins and other materials connected to African diasporic spirituality. “I place my ancestors into new visual and spiritual contexts— ones that center dignity, protection, and possibility,” Broxton said. “Sequins and beads function as both adornment and armor, transforming each portrait into a site of reverence, where absence becomes space for reimagining.” Broxton’s exhibition is on view now through August 16. Visit https://www.moadsf.org/ exhibitions/ancestral-echoes for more information.
articles.title: Demetri Broxton: Ancestral Echoes on view now at MoAD

The museum’s latest exhibition, Mildred Howard: Poetics of Memory, will be on view alongside special festival programming. articles.text: Henri Matisse’s Femme au chapeau is the highlight of SFMOMA’s newest exhibition. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is presenting a new exhibition focused on Henri Matisse’s Femme au chapeau, a painting widely regarded as a landmark of modern art. The exhibition, titled Matisse’s Femme au chapeau: A Modern Scandal, opened May 16 and is on view through September. The exhibition examines the history, reception and lasting influence of the 1905 portrait, which is part of SFMOMA’s permanent collection. The painting debuted at the Salon d’Automne in Paris in 1905 and became associated with Fauvism, the first French avantgarde art movement of the 20th century. The exhibition explores the work’s historical context, subject, provenance and circulation through exhibitions and publications, while also considering its impact on later generations of artists. “We are thrilled to have this opportunity to share the full story of Matisse’s Femme au chapeau—a painting that is emblematic of the artist’s radical break from convention in the early years of his career,” Janet Bishop, SFMOMA Chief Curator, said in a press release. “Arguably SFMOMA’s most art-historically significant work of art, Femme au chapeau began sending shockwaves through the art world as soon as it left Matisse’s studio and has captivated viewers ever since,” Bishop added. The exhibition also traces the painting’s ownership history. American collectors Leo and Gertrude Stein acquired the work in 1905 while living in Paris. It later entered the collection of Michael and Sarah Stein, who brought it to the Bay Area in 1935. The painting was first exhibited in the United States at the San Francisco Museum of Art, now SFMOMA, in 1936. It entered the museum’s collection in 1991 through a bequest from Elise S. Haas. “Part of our vision at SFMOMA is to encourage our visitors to see the world—and art—in new ways,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “With stunning paintings by Matisse and his peers, as well as work by some of the most exceptional artists working today, this exhibition promises to captivate SFMOMA visitors this spring.” Visit https://www.sfmoma. org/ for more information. ®

The play is set in an English village in 1926 where gossip is the local currency. When the widowed Mrs Ferrars is found dead by apparent suicide and shortly after he fiancé, the most prominent man in town – Roger Ackroyd, is found dead the rumors start to run rampant and the local police are stumped. However, it just so happens that the villages newest resident is world famous detective Hercule Poirot, who sets out to find the truth and find the murderer. The production is directed and designed by Matt Cardigan Smith and features local Piedmont resident Maya Rath as Gertrude Ackroyd. articles.text: The San Francisco Opera celebrates Pride Month on Friday, June 26 at the War Memorial Opera House, featuring a program of opera, musical theater and popular music alongside community exhibits, discussions and a post-concert dance party. The event will be hosted by drag performer, opera singer and composer Sapphira Cristal, who returns as emcee following last year’s inaugural concert. Conductor Robert Mollicone will lead the San Francisco Opera Orchestra and soloists Melody Moore, Nikola Printz and Reginald Smith Jr. The concert will feature works by composers and artists including Michael Abels, Terence Blanchard, Brandi Carlile, Umberto Giordano, Charles Gounod, k.d. lang, Jacques Offenbach, Stephen Schwartz, Michael Tilson Thomas, Luther Vandross and Stevie Wonder. The evening’s activities begin at 6:30 p.m. before the performance with a pride-themed altar created by the Marigold Project, a happy hour, educational exhibits and a pre-concert discussion featuring creators of the Rainbow Pride Flag Project. Additional displays will be presented by the GLBT Historical Society, the Hand Bookbinders of California and the National AIDS Memorial, which will exhibit panels from the AIDS Memorial Quilt. The concert begins at 8 p.m. Following the performance, attendees can participate in a dance party featuring DJ Juanita MORE!. The Pride Concert is part of a broader weekend of Pride celebrations for the company. On June 28, members of San Francisco Opera will join other arts organizations in the 56th annual San Francisco Pride Parade along Market Street. Visit https://www.sfopera. com/seasons/pride-concert-2026/ to purchase tickets. The War Memorial House hosts its second Pride concert on Friday, June 26.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Michael Stehr Artist and art historian Michael Stehr’s recent lecture on Monet in Venice was brilliantly informative. The information should be factored into every musical performance. Discovering the interconnection of the arts can be a challenge. Sometimes the discovery is made obliquely. That was the case on Saturday afternoon during a lecture by the gifted artist and art lecturer Michael Stehr who grew up in Piedmont. Saturday’s lecture was about Monet in Venice. You could take it at face value, and walk away with the information that Monet was a great artist. That’s enough for lots of people. But Michael Stehr opened the world of the arts to his audience. He enlightened his audience in a marvelous way by making us understand exactly why Monet was representative of great art. articles.text: Finnish choir Vox Aurea Vox Aurea choir, established in 1968, is the flagship choir of the City of Jyväskylä’s education services in Finland. The choir is attending the Golden Gate International Choral Festival hosted by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. Vox Aurea’s spotlight performance is on July 17 at the Central Chinese High School Victory Hall in San Francisco. The choir will also participate in the group performances on the opening and closing nights. The choir has participated in numerous national and international competitions, receiving several awards. Vox Aurea has also released numerous recordings that showcase the diversity of choral music. The choir is made up of 50 singers aged 11 to 19. Before joining Vox Aurea, these singers usually perform in preparatory choirs that are open to children as young as three. The choir’s vocal coach is Josefiina Fagerlund. Alongside its educational work, Vox Aurea actively engages in local, national, and international collaboration, while also promoting Finnish and international choral music. Commissioning new works from contemporary composers is an established part of the choir’s activity. Their most recent recording, Pato (released in December 2020), features a collection of works commissioned by Vox Aurea during the 2010s. Sanna Salminen became the conductor of Vox Aurea in 2009. Salminen has worked for the choir since 1998 as the voice trainer and assistant conductor, collaborating intensively with Pekka Kostiainen, the previous conductor. Salminen works as a university teacher at the Department of Music, Art and Culture Studies at the University of Jyväskylä. In 2014, Salminen was awarded the Golden Medal of Merit of the Finnish Youth Choirs Association. In the anniversary year of Vox Aurea in 2018, Salminen was awarded the Heinz Hofmann Medal of the Finnish Youth Choirs Association and the Medal of Merit of the Sulasol Central Finland District. Collaboration with youth choirs from different countries is an essential part of Vox Aurea’s work. Through these exchanges, the choir has broadened its repertoire, deepened its understanding of choral traditions across cultures, and further developed its pedagogical and strategic practices. In recent years, Vox Aurea has had the privilege of working with choreographer Daniel Raaflaub from Basel, Switzerland, whose contribution has elevated the choir’s expressive performance to a new level. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place from July 13 to July 18. articles.text: Curry Barker’s record-breaking indie film follows a music store employee (Michael Johnston) that makes a wish for his friend Nikki (Inde Navarette) to fall in love with him, only for it to go terribly wrong. The movie gained traction when a short clip of Inde Navarette’s acting earned thousands of views on TikTok and Instagram, translating to over 280 million dollars in the box office. The emotional outburst that made an impact on scrollers is only a glimpse into Barker’s twisted, supernatural world. If you are a fan of horror, this is a film that you will want to go watch. Just remember to be careful what you wish for… There are many choices that the filmmakers put in place to create an unsettling atmosphere. The color grading is one of those choices. While many films in the genre often use muted or cold tones, Obsession takes a different approach. The movie is colorful, and its shots are often warmly tinted, especially in yellow. It feels almost unnatural, which provides foreshadowing to the film’s events. Then there’s the use of shadow, and the use of silence, which both make the viewer uneasy before (and during) big scares. From these trends to the tiny details, it is clear that a lot of thought has gone into the film. Production, however, is just one piece of the puzzle. What really makes the movie such an Inde Navarrette and Michael Johnston in Obsession unexpected success is the stellar acting. Navarette’s strongest point is her facial expressions: under the influence of the wish, her smile (often put up around Bear, Johnston’s character) looks unnatural, and her deep frown is even creepier. Her “obsession” is apparent, but the wrongness of it all is made even more clear by the way she moves around the world. It is safe to say that she terrified everyone in the theater, and at the same time, the viewer couldn’t help but feel bad for the person under the enchantment. Put together, the response was clear. Sitting in the theater, it was common to hear gasps, whispers, and even screams. To be fair, a lot of them were coming from me. It provided the scare of a lifetime, and while I wouldn’t bring my younger brother or my grandmother to see it (definitely NOT family friendly) I did enjoy it. Obsession is projected to stay in theaters into July, around a month longer than originally slotted. Its extended run is a testament to the fact that audiences are loving it, and it is absolutely worth watching if you enjoy being terrified, if you’re brave enough. Be sure to catch it at the Landmark Theater on Piedmont Avenue or the Grand Lake before its run ends. Obsession. Directed by Curry Barker. Starring Michael Johnston, Inde Navarrette, Cooper Tomlinson, Megan Lawless and Andy Richter. Released in 2026. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated R. In theaters; not yet streaming, with Peacock expected later in 2026 Mira Sen is a rising Junior at Head-Royce School

articles.text: The acclaimed post-apocalyptic film The Road is based on the Pulitzer Prize-winning novel by Cormac McCarthy (2006) whose spare prose and remarkable story telling has often been adapted for the screen by Hollywood’s directors and writers. When this film released in 2008, it received multiple nominations and awards, while some critics opined that it affirmed that film was an extraordinary medium, a nexus of sorts, able to capture and reflect upon the human condition. It was an art. Essential to that art were the actors who inhabit a character with all attendant emotions and reactions, no matter the context and range. Viggo Mortensen portrays Papa/the father, and Kodi Smit-McPhee is his young son, each are each remarkable as was the cameo appearance by Charlize Theron as the wife and mother. Viggo Mortensen and Kodi Smit-McPhee in The Road The film was was shot by cinematographer Javier Aguirresarobe, who captured its haunting, stark images with a kind of counter-intuitive depth and beauty. As the story unfolds, we realize that what has occurred is revealed only through the father and son’s journey, making their way along this post-apocalyptic road. They push a shopping cart that contains all they possess (the father does carry a hidden revolver with only two bullets in its chambers). Both are gaunt, their clothes little more than frayed rags; they are walking south, toward an ocean they can only imagine. The sky is leaden, forbidding, the forests blackened by fires, and enormous trees suddenly crash to the ground. A cold, misty rain follows them. The father is stalked by a relentless cough, his restless sleep haunted by fevered dreams of the past, his thoughts shared in a halting voice-over. Both are ever in search of food, and remain apprehensive, watching, always alert when passing through abandoned homes and broken towns. Those few who have survived can suddenly appear, some driven by panic and fear, others by an absence of all restraint and any semblance of humanity, their desperation framed by the unthinkable. And so, father and son walk on, nurturing a fragile hope. The boy, having seen more than any child can comprehend, asks his father: “Papa, we’re still the good guys, aren’t we?” His question, a need to know – do they still possess a morality that for those they encounter has long ago been discarded now ruled by a Darwinian struggle to survive. If you’re reading the above and wondering why you should seek out tis film, perhaps questioning why it would be critically praised, well, I understand. But post-apocalyptic films, some touching on sci-fi, are a solid, perhaps nihilistic filmmaking genre. Many are cautionary tales, asking the audience to consider the unintended consequences of our collective actions and behaviors and their aftermath. If the earth is our mother, are we slowly, inexplicably committing matricide? The Road. Directed by John Hillcoat. With Viggo Mortensen, Kodi Smit-McPhee, Charlize Theron. Based on a book by Cormac McCarthy. 1 hr., 59 min. Rated R. Released in 2008. Now streaming on Prime/YouTube/ Fandango/Hulu.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group gathered last Wednesday at the Exedra on a warm morning that was forecast to be a “Piedmont hot” day. There was a large turnout of 50 walkers and five K-9 best friends in attendance. The big turnout owed to the day’s destination: a pool party. The group hadn’t been up to the Huntleigh and Lexford loop off Hampton Road this year, and walker and realtor Stacey Isaacs had a home for sale at 11 Huntleigh Road. She wanted to show the group the house and its swimming pool. The walkers started off behind the Exedra, past the Community Hall and Tea House, and up the Highland-Guilford steps in the upper part of Piedmont Park. They emerged on Highland Avenue, crossed it, and walked the path along the long strip of grass that was once a Key System train right of way. Parked in front of the grass was one of the biggest moving vans most walkers had ever seen. The group continued up Sheridan Avenue to Wildwood Avenue, the Hall Fenway, Crocker Avenue, and Hampton Road. Along Hampton, just before Sea View Avenue, a construction project was underway. A big, deep space had been carved out of the land next to a house. The walkers guessed it might be an ADU, but a worker said no, it would be a new garage. articles.text: Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on October 13, 2021 One of the delights that comes from walking around town is discovering and actually reading the many commemorative plaques located in Piedmont. Apparently originating in the Middle Ages, historical interest groups at all levels of governments all over the world seem to have their own commemorative system of celebrating the connection of a location with a special event, person or structure. These range from a very coordinated, consistent aesthetic such as on the blue ceramic heritage plaques found throughout all of England, to the more common mixed styles found in the U.S. including Piedmont. Since the majority are quite often outside in the weather, what they all have in common is durability. Many are made of different long lasting materials such as bronze, marble, stone and zinc to name a few. Brass is however probably the most common material because of its shiny, gold-colored appearance, strength and low maintenance. Historical plaques are most often mounted to a wall, One of the most interesting “historical” plaques in town is the one marking the Piedmont Community Church’s time capsule. Buried in the main courtyard arcade, it is scheduled to be unearthed in 2035. large stone or other vertical surface. However, like many things in our age of more information and resulting reevaluation, commemorating history can now be a contentious issue. When we find out more about the dark side of celebrated historical figures, what has resulted in some cases is the removal of older plaques and statues—sometimes rightly so. This suggests that a more thorough evaluation and vetting of honorees going forward would be wise. Exclusive focus on certain genders, races or those of special status seems to be a thing of the past. It is interesting, and maybe a little sad, that studies have shown that most commemoratives (statues and monuments) generally go unnoticed after a time, probably because of simple familiarity. But I think they can be, and always will be a valuable addition to our built environment. Even though we may not be readily able to recall certain of them, I think we would certainly readily notice We have discussed the beauty, function and importance of urban design in previous columns. A city that understands these concepts should indeed honor the people who support them and make them possible. These appropriate, well-designed and well deserved plaques themselves add interest and punctuation to the urban design of the city. Piedmont’s Centennial House plaques rest on 173 homes, all built before city incorporation in 1907 and judged to have maintained the architectural style and character of the original buildings. The Wetmore house, adjacent to City Hall, is on the National Register of Historic Places. A similar sub-category of historical plaques are “donor bricks” such as this nice installation honoring the supporters of Witter Field construction. Memorial benches, found throughout the parks of Piedmont, add interesting detail as well as a welcome place to relax.

We can’t wait to watch her grow here at Oakland Zoo,” said Oakland Zoo Animal Care Keeper Jessica Parke. This move follows a recommendation from the Association of Zoos and Aquariums’ (AZA) Species Survival Plan (SSP) to improve breeding success and animal welfare. Kendi, another two-year-old female giraffe at Oakland Zoo, now has a companion her age, an important part of supporting her overall wellbeing. Having a peer of the same age allows Kendi to grow up alongside another juvenile. In the wild, female giraffes often form strong social bonds, spending much of their lives together and developing friendships. They also often babysit and help raise one another’s calves. This partnership provides all the giraffes in Oakland Zoo’s herd with increased opportunities for natural behaviors such as play and more complex social relationships, mirroring those of a typical giraffe herd. It also gives females multiple “sisters” to help them raise their calves. Joann comes from a decadeslong lineage of giraffes rooted in the Bay Area, including those at Oakland Zoo. She and Maggie come from the same family tree: Tiki, a beloved Oakland Zoo giraffe who has since passed, had five offspring during her time at the Oakland Zoo, including Dadisi, Joann’s grandmother, who moved as a juvenile from Oakland to Palm Desert as part of the AZA’s Species Survival Plan. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors’ latest excursion was to Livermore, and was educational, exciting, and fulfilling. The first stop was at the Lawrence Livermore Discovery Center – a true destination for inspiration! The Discovery Center offers in-person visitors an exciting glimpse into cutting-edge science and technology. The featured exhibits showcase the Laboratory’s state-of-the-art research programs, which range from high-performance computing, to bioscience and bioengineering, to advanced materials and manufacturing. They are designed to inspire the next generation of researchers by showcasing new innovations and the impactful work conducted at the Lab. Different areas of the Discovery Center feature such items as a Heritage of Innovation, Forensic Science, Biotechnology, Seismology, and there is a booth where the Seniors could test their knowledge with multiple choice questions using computers. Senior members had the opportunity to learn about energy and climate science by hopping on an energy bike to learn how much “pedal power” it takes to turn on a lightbulb, They also got a taste of Lawrence Livermore Lab’s contributions to climate science research. The Laboratory opened on September 2, 1952, initially as a branch of the University of California Radiation Laboratory. Prior to the Lab’s opening, this parcel of land was the site of the Livermore Naval Air Station, a World War II pilot training facility. Throughout its history, the Laboratory has fulfilled its national security mission, establishing itself as a hallmark of cutting-edge science and technology in service to society. After this educational visit, the Members of the Piedmont Seniors had the opportunity to step into a replica of the National Ignition Facility target chamber, which “brings star power to earth. They include (L to R): Nancy Everett, Nancy Hinsch, Sandra Ponce, Susan McCreary, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Gloria Wilmer, and Elizabeth Wierzbianska. The Piedmont Seniors visited the Lawrence Livermore Discovery Center. Pictured are (seated in front): Arlene Garfinkle; (L to R): James Ayotte, Sue Getreuer, Edith Hereso, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Gloria Wilmer, Sandra Ponce, Nancy Hinsch, and Susan McCreary; (back row): Greg Jurin, Fred Pemberton, and Nancy Everett. Seniors then turned the page as its next venture was to the Bankhead Theater in downtown Livermore to take in a Tri-Valley lighthearted production of Newsies: The Broadway Musical. The cast of this almost-three-hour musical was entirely that of teenagers, and they did an outstanding job. Their singing, dancing, and gymnastics was a pleasure to watch. Afterwards, the Seniors then ventured to Terra Mia Cucina Italiana for a cross between lunch and dinner – “linner”. This restaurant definitely was able to tickle the Seniors’ taste buds with playful culinary creations. It was an excellent way to “put the cherry on top” of a delightful, educational, and fun-filled day. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I am so frustrated with keeping track of my passwords. Now when I enter a password on a website like PayPal, I get a window asking if I would like to use a passkey. I don’t understand the difference between passwords and passkeys. Is this just one more thing I have to keep track of? I am already losing the battle with remembering all of my passwords and keeping them in a safe place. Felix, Oakland Dear Felix: You are not alone for sure. Passwords are one of the most important and frustrating aspects of the digital world. With all of the phishing attacks, security breaches and computer scams it seems we are constantly under threat of identity theft, credit card fraud and scams. And most of us don’t really have the skills to make a password that is not easily guessed, or accessible through data breaches. The creation of passkeys is supposed to make all of these vulnerabilities harder to crack. Passwords are strings of characters that we (or our password apps) create to use to access secure websites like our bank, PayPal, shopping sites, etc. Passkeys on the other hand, are system-generated cryptographic key pairs. Instead of typing and having to remember a password, your system creates passkeys to unlock and enable your various accounts using your device’s built-in security, such as Face ID, Touch ID, your log in password or a pin code. For this to work, iCloud Keychain must be turned on in your Mac, iPhone and iPad settings, which syncs your passkeys across all your Apple devices. To do this • Open the Apple Menu > System Settings (or System Preferences). • Click your Apple ID (or name) at the top. • Click iCloud > Passwords & Keychain and make sure it is turned If you are signing into a new website account, put in a username and submit. When you get the option to create a passkey, choose the method you would like to use to sign in, Touch ID, Face ID or “other options” such as a QR code (from a nearby device such as your iPhone) or an external security key. If you don’t want to have to remember or keep track of a key code, then Touch ID or Face ID is fine. If you want to change your password on a site to a passkey, log in as you normally do, then go to the Passwords and Security section and look for the option to, “register a passkey,” “use passkey,” or “sign in with a passkey.” The website will prompt you to save a passkey to your Mac. You will then use Touch ID or your Mac’s password to save the passkey to your Mac. The use of passkeys is replacing user generated passwords for several reasons. They are much more secure than passwords. Passwords are vulnerable to phishing and data breaches, whereas passkeys are mathematically impossible to guess and are strictly tied to the legitimate website or app, providing complete immunity to phishing. Passwords also require databases on the website’s server to authenticate, and passkeys use asymmetric cryptography: a “public key” is kept by the website, while the “private key” never leaves your device’s secure hardware. And you no longer must remember hundreds of passwords, you just have to know how to securely get into your computer account, which most of us do each day when we log in with either our computer log in password or touch ID. So when that window pops up asking if you would like to create a passkey, just enable it by clicking “continue”. You will then be prompted to use your Touch ID or enter your Mac’s login password. The passkey will then be stored in your iCloud keychain. articles.text: Anyone familiar with dogs will agree that canine companions are incredibly talented. From pet dogs who put a smile on their owners’ faces, to search and rescue dogs who save lives, dogs have an abundance of admirable skills. Many of those skills are grounded in their sense of smell, which is estimated to be 10,000 to 100,000 times more acute than our own. Thanks to this skill, an incredible type of service dog is becoming more common: the migraine alert dog. Migraines have cycles and the first symptoms, during the “prodrome phase,” can appear as early as a few days before any excruciating pain. Here, the enzymes in saliva start to change from their normal state; it is here that dogs begin to smell the change. At this point, a trained migraine alert dog will signal their handler, usually by pawing or booping with the nose, allowing the handler to take medication early enough to mitigate the migraine. A service dog can signal in many ways, but a pawing motion is most commonly taught because it is unusual enough to grab a handler’s attention. To teach the dog to detect the enzymatic change in saliva, the owner is asked to collect saliva samples with cotton balls when they have migraines. The samples are stored in sealed jars and labeled the date, symptoms and intensity of the migraine on a 1-10 scale. The jars are then stored in the freezer to preserve the scent. In training, a dog is shown a sample and given a verbal command to paw once they smell the sample; they are rewarded when they signal with a pawing motion. This is repeated until the dog begins to signal on their own. In order to teach the dog that they should signal for specific scents and not the presentation of the jar, control samples (samples with no saliva) are used. Once the dog shows nearly 100% consistency, the owner transitions to breathing across the sample. This teaches the dog where to expect the source of the target scent in a daily environment. Eventually, the dog will signal their handler whenever they smell the change on the owner’s breath, despite distractions and even the presence of enticing smells like food. Migraine alert training is a life-enhancing option for people who suffer from migraines. Dogs
